What the official sources say

  • Primary and nonprimary residential property is valued at 9 percent of assessed value for taxable value. (N.D.C.C. 57-02-27(1)(a); source)
  • Assessor must deliver written notice of true and full value at least 15 days before the local board of equalization meeting; notice must give the local and county board meeting dates. (N.D.C.C. 57-02-53; source)
  • Township and city boards of equalization meet in April (dates set by the board; confirm with county or city auditor). (Property Tax Deadlines | ND Office of State Tax Commissioner; source)
  • The county board of equalization meets within the first 10 days of June; owners may appear personally, by representative, or appeal by mail or other communication stating reasons. (N.D.C.C. 57-12-01, 57-12-06; source)
  • The State Board of Equalization meets the second Tuesday in August for locally assessed property; individual taxpayers may speak and submit written material or photographs. To file, contact the Property Tax division (propertytax@nd.gov, 701-328-3127). (State Board of Equalization | ND Office of State Tax Commissioner; source)
  • After foreclosure date, county auditor issues a tax deed to the county, passing title free of encumbrances except specified special assessments, homestead credit lien and recorded easements. (N.D.C.C. 57-28-09; source)
  • County sells at annual auction to highest qualified bidder at or above minimum price, cash or one-fourth down with balance up to 10 years; interest not over 12%; bidders owing delinquent county taxes are disqualified. (N.D.C.C. 57-28-15; source)

Who sets and collects property tax in North Dakota?

Counties determine and collect property tax on real property and mobile homes, then pass the money to the county, cities, townships, school districts and other taxing districts. The State Tax Commissioner publishes the calendar and runs the state boards, but a homeowner pays the county treasurer.

The tax comes from three inputs: the mill rate, the taxable value and the taxing entity. Real property is assessed as of February 1, and assessed value is 50 percent of market value, which the Tax Commissioner describes as what the property would sell for in the current market. The county auditor builds the tax list and delivers it to the treasurer by December 10, and the treasurer must mail a statement by December 26.

When are North Dakota property taxes due, and what are the penalties?

Real estate tax is due on January 1 following the year it was levied and becomes delinquent after March 1 for a single payment or the first installment. Under N.D.C.C. 57-20-01, unpaid first-installment tax picks up a 3 percent penalty after March 1 and another 3 percent on May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment becomes delinquent after October 15 and takes a 6 percent penalty.

DateWhat it means
January 1Tax for the prior levy year is due
February 15Pay all of the year's tax by this date for a 5 percent discount
March 1Last day for the first installment without penalty
October 15Last day for the second installment without penalty
November 1Deadline to apply for abatement of the earlier year's tax
December 26Treasurers mail the new tax statements

If a due date lands on a day the treasurer's office is closed, payment on the next open day carries no penalty and no loss of discount. A missing statement is no excuse: the statute says failure to receive one does not relieve the owner or extend the February 15 discount deadline.

How does the 5 percent early-payment discount work?

The county treasurer allows a 5 percent discount to taxpayers who pay all of a parcel's real estate tax for the year in full on or before February 15. The discount applies to general taxes for the state, county, city, township, school district and other districts, but not to special assessment installments, and it is applied before the Primary Residence Credit.

  • A county commission can extend the discount period by 30 days if it finds a weather or other emergency.
  • Installments must be at least 10 percent of the tax and never less than $10.
  • Discounts do not apply to payment on property that has delinquent tax.

Payments on a parcel with older tax owed go first to the oldest delinquent amount, with its penalty and interest, which matters for a seller who is catching up before closing.

How can you appeal a North Dakota assessment?

An owner can appeal through a chain of equalization boards that meet in a fixed order during the spring and summer. The assessor must deliver written notice of the value at least 15 days before the local board of equalization meets, and the notice gives the dates of the local and county board meetings.

  • Township and city boards of equalization meet in April, on dates set locally. Confirm the date with the county or city auditor.
  • The county board of equalization meets within the first 10 days of June. Owners may appear personally, send a representative, or appeal by mail stating reasons.
  • The State Board of Equalization meets the second Tuesday in August for locally assessed property. Individuals can speak and submit written material or photographs, and the Property Tax division can be reached at propertytax@nd.gov or 701-328-3127.

An owner who disagrees with a bill after it is issued has two more routes. Tax can be paid under protest to the county treasurer with written reasons, and the owner then has 60 days to apply to the county commissioners for abatement, adjustment or a refund. The separate abatement application for an earlier year's tax is due by November 1.

Which credits lower a North Dakota homeowner's bill?

Three state credits can reduce what a homeowner owes. The Primary Residence Credit is up to $1,600 against the tax due, for an owner who lives in a house, mobile home, town home, duplex or condo as a primary residence, with no age or income limits. A homeowner can also hold the Homestead or Disabled Veteran's credit and still use the Primary Residence Credit on any remaining balance.

CreditKey terms
Primary Residence CreditUp to $1,600, cannot exceed the tax due; applications open in January and close April 1
Homestead Property Tax CreditApplicant age 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled; income of $70,000 or less in the year before the assessment date
Disabled Veteran's Property Tax CreditReduces taxable value by up to $9,000 at a 100 percent rating; portable to a new homestead

The credits are tied to an owner who lives in the home, so a buyer who moves in files a new application of their own.

What happens when North Dakota property tax goes unpaid?

The unpaid tax becomes a lien, and the county can foreclose it and take the property by tax deed after at least two years. Between November 1 and 15 each year, the treasurer mails a notice to the owner of each delinquent parcel stating that the tax is a lien and that foreclosure follows unless the amount is paid by October 1 of the second year after the tax became delinquent.

The auditor gives notice of foreclosure by June 1. The foreclosure date is October 1 after service, and the tax deed then passes the property to the county free of most encumbrances. Section 57-28-04 adds foreclosure costs of $50 or actual costs, whichever is higher, to the amount needed to clear the lien. A residential property gets personal service by the sheriff if the owner lives in the state.

Tax deed land is appraised, then sold at auction starting the third Tuesday in November for cash or one-fourth down with the balance over up to ten years. The former owner, the owner's executor, or a parent, spouse or child may repurchase while the county still holds title. If the sale brings in more than the taxes and costs, the excess is held 90 days for the record owner to claim.

How does tax due at closing work for a seller?

The unpaid tax, penalty and interest come out of the seller's proceeds at closing, and the county treasurer applies the money to the oldest year first. A title company will check the treasurer's records for current and delinquent tax, and for special assessments, which are billed with the tax.

  • Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure before the closing date.
  • Check the first and second installment status for the year, since the second is not delinquent until after October 15.
  • Ask whether any special assessment installments are outstanding.
  • If the house was inherited, confirm who received the tax statement, since it goes to one owner at the last-known address.

How the current year's tax is split between buyer and seller is a term of the purchase contract. A short closing timeline helps most when a lien notice has already been mailed, because the October 1 foreclosure date is fixed by statute.

More questions about North Dakota Property Tax Guide

What is the North Dakota property tax due date?

Real estate tax is due January 1 and is delinquent after March 1. It may be paid in two installments, with the second due without penalty through October 15, and a 5 percent discount applies if all of it is paid by February 15.

What penalty applies to late North Dakota property tax?

First-installment tax takes a 3 percent penalty after March 1, with another 3 percent on May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment takes a 6 percent penalty after October 15.

How do I appeal my North Dakota property assessment?

Start with the township or city board of equalization in April, then the county board in the first 10 days of June, then the State Board of Equalization in August. Assessment notices must reach you at least 15 days before the local board meets.

How much is the North Dakota Primary Residence Credit?

Up to $1,600 against the property tax due, with no age or income limit, for an owner who lives in the home. The application deadline is April 1.

Can I sell a house in North Dakota if I owe property tax?

Yes. The tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, oldest year first. Selling before the foreclosure date also keeps the county from taking the property by tax deed.
